state.misconception_label: Has used slant height and base to find area of a triangle rather than perpendicular height and base

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: How would you calculate the area of this triangle? ![A triangle, base 12m. All three sides are equal.](). I got \( \frac{12 \times 12}{2} \) because I added the side lengths instead of multiplying.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Great job recognizing that you need to multiply the base and height to find the area of a triangle! In this case, make sure to use the perpendicular height instead of the slant height. Can you think about how to find the perpendicular height in this triangle with all three sides being equal?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so I need to use the perpendicular height, not just any side of the triangle. Um, so for this equilateral triangle, would I need to draw a line straight down from the top to the base? But how do I actually work out what that height is if all the sides are 12m?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: You're on the right track! Since you have an equilateral triangle, all three sides are equal, which means you can use the properties of an equilateral triangle to find the perpendicular height. Remember, the perpendicular height divides the equilateral triangle into two 30-60-90 right triangles. Can you think of a relationship between the sides of a 30-60-90 triangle that could help you find the perpendicular height in this case?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, I'm not really sure about 30-60-90 triangles... Is that something to do with the angles? So when I draw the line down the middle, it creates two smaller triangles, and those have special angle measurements? Could you maybe explain what the relationship between the sides is, because I'm a bit confused about how that helps me find the height?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher clearly addresses the perpendicular vs. slant height misconception, but the scaffolding overshoots the student's knowledge (30-60-90 triangles are unfamiliar), and while the student recognizes they need perpendicular height, they remain unable to calculate it by Turn 4.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher attempts to scaffold by breaking down the problem, they introduce 30-60-90 triangles without assessing whether this is within the student's Zone of Proximal Development, and when the student explicitly signals confusion about this concept in Turn 4, the teacher has not adjusted their support level appropriately.
